title: Zen comes west
hookLine: teachers like D. T. Suzuki carry Zen to Western readers

cards: A story told in Zen circles. A learned visitor comes to a Zen teacher to ask about Zen. The teacher serves tea, pouring into the cup until it's full, and keeps pouring.
Tea runs over the rim and across the table. Stop, says the visitor, nothing more will go in. Like this cup, the teacher answers, you are full of your own opinions.
How can I show you Zen unless you first empty your cup? Stories like that crossed the ocean in books, and some Western readers met Zen first on the page.

teach.b: Remember the young layman who helped Soyen Shaku with his English in Chicago? D. T.
Suzuki had trained in Zen under that abbot in Kamakura. Afterward he went to America and spent years there translating and writing.
He wrote about Zen in English, in essays and translations, and later lectured to university audiences.

Readers who had never met a Zen teacher met Zen through him: the sudden awakenings, the strange questions, the teachers who answered with a shout. What crossed most easily were the short stories, like the cup of tea.

Zen describes itself with a saying tradition gives to Bodhidharma, whom we met on the road through China: a special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words, pointing straight at the mind.
There's a gentle joke in that. A tradition that says it doesn't depend on words reached the West through a great many of them. But Zen keeps pointing past the book.
The stories are meant to unsettle the mind that thinks it already knows, and the tradition's answer to that unsettled mind is to sit.

teach.h: FROM THE BOOK TO THE CUSHION.
teach.b: So the books were followed by people. Japanese teachers came west to lead sittings, and Western students went to Japan to train in monasteries and came home to teach.
A cup of tea in a book, then real cups of tea in real meditation halls, across the ocean.

how: Zen communities in the West sit together in meditation halls, often under teachers trained in Japan or in lineages that came from there, and read short Zen stories as part of their study.

o: a Zen student who wrote about Zen in English
a Japanese abbot who spoke in Chicago
a Zen master who founded temples in California

games.q: Zen comes west: tap the pairs.

s: D. T. Suzuki learned about Zen only from books
he trained in Zen under the abbot Soyen Shaku in Kamakura.
in the story, the teacher stops pouring when the cup is full
he keeps pouring until the tea runs over.
Western students went to Japan to train and came home to teach
the books were followed by people who sat.

games.q: you're the teacher. a learned guest has come to ask about Zen, and he's full of opinions. what do you do?
o: pour his tea until it overflows.
games.why: in the story, the teacher keeps pouring until the cup overflows, then says the guest is just as full.

practice: Go through the cup of tea once more in your mind, the pouring, the tea running over, empty your cup, then set the story down and meet the next breath as if it were the first you'd ever noticed.
When the mind starts to say, I know this already, let a little tea spill over the rim, and come back to the breath that's actually here.

wordCard.voice: Suzuki. D. T. Suzuki, the Zen student whose books and lectures carried the teaching to America, and the stories like the cup of tea.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhyana: meditation, the practice Zen keeps pointing back to, past the books.

carryVoice: Your line: across the ocean. The book points past itself, to the cushion. Day nine hundred forty-eight.
